units.title: Unit 13 — Family and friends
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate, Fourth Edition
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Identify relatives, including step-relations, siblings, nieces, nephews, cousins, and in-laws.
Distinguish widow, remarriage, close family, only child, and elder and younger siblings.
Use possessive constructions such as Thomas’s wife naturally.
Describe friendship and relationship history using get to know, get on well with, ever since, and ex-.
Use informal mate and expressions for friends, former partners, and getting married.

items.example: We invited our relatives to lunch on Sunday.
items.note: Members of your family; relations has the same meaning.

items.example: Many of my relations live abroad.
items.note: Relations can mean family members as well as connections between people.

items.example: After her husband died, she became a widow.
items.note: A woman whose husband has died; compare widower for a man.

items.example: My grandfather decided to remarry several years later.
items.note: Marry again after a previous marriage has ended.

items.example: My stepfather helps me with my homework.
items.note: Your mother's husband who is not your biological father.

items.example: Her stepfather is kind, and she also sees her real father.
items.note: Here real father refers to a person's biological father.

items.example: I call my uncle by his first name.
items.note: The name given to you, rather than your family name.

items.word: call someone by their first name
items.example: At work, we call our manager by her first name.
items.note: A natural construction for saying how you address someone informally.

items.example: My elder sister lives in Bristol.
items.note: Common before a family noun such as brother or sister; older is more general.

items.example: My elder brother has just started a new job.
items.note: Elder is used particularly to compare siblings.

items.example: My younger sister is still at school.
items.note: Younger is a natural way to describe a sibling's relative age.

items.example: The twins were born on the same day.
items.note: Two children born to the same mother at one birth.

items.example: We're a close family and meet regularly.
items.note: A family whose members have strong, supportive relationships.

items.example: She's an only child, so she has no siblings.
items.note: A person who has no brothers or sisters.

items.example: My uncle lives near the coast.
items.note: A parent's brother, or the husband of a parent's sibling.

items.example: I often visit my cousins during the holidays.
items.note: A child of your aunt or uncle; cousin is used for both sexes.

items.example: My nephew is learning to ride a bike.
items.note: The son of your brother or sister.

items.example: My niece turned ten last month.
items.note: The daughter of your brother or sister.

items.example: My sister-in-law is a nurse.
items.note: The sister of your spouse, or the wife of your sibling.

items.example: My brother-in-law is married to my younger sister.
items.note: The brother of your spouse, or the husband of your sibling.

items.example: My mother-in-law is coming to dinner.
items.note: The mother of your husband or wife; an example of the -in-law family.

items.pt: do lado do meu pai; por parte de pai
items.example: I have several cousins on my father's side.
items.note: Refers to relatives connected through one parent.

items.pt: dar-se bem com; ter bom relacionamento com
items.example: I get on well with both of my sisters.
items.note: Get on well with someone means have a good relationship with them.

items.example: This photograph is my favourite.
items.note: British spelling: favourite; a preferred person or thing.

items.example: There are nine grandchildren altogether.
items.note: Means in total; different from all together, meaning in one group.

items.pt: casado e com filhos; casada e com filhos
items.example: She's married with two children.
items.note: A common descriptive pattern meaning married and having children.

items.example: Thomas's wife works in a hospital.
items.note: Use possessive 's naturally with people, rather than the wife of Thomas.

items.example: My best friend has known me since primary school.
items.note: The friend you are closest to.

items.pt: amigo antigo da escola; amiga antiga da escola
items.example: I met an old school friend at the station.
items.note: A person you knew at school a long time ago; old refers to the friendship.

items.example: It takes time to get to know new colleagues.
items.note: Gradually become familiar with someone; not the same as know already.

items.pt: conhecer-se melhor; passar a conhecer um ao outro
items.example: We got to know each other on the training course.
items.note: Used when two people gradually become acquainted.

items.example: I'm meeting a mate for coffee this afternoon.
items.note: Informal British English for friend.

items.example: We met at school and have been friends ever since.
items.note: Refers to a period continuing from a past point until now.

items.example: Their friendship has lasted for twenty years.
items.note: The relationship between friends.

items.example: Her current address is in Manchester.
items.note: Current refers to the present, not the past.

items.example: His current girlfriend also enjoys cycling.
items.note: Current distinguishes a present partner from an ex-partner.

items.example: He is still friends with his ex-girlfriend.
items.note: The prefix ex- marks a previous relationship that has ended.

items.example: She sometimes sees her ex-boyfriend at university.
items.note: The ex- prefix means former or previous.

items.example: Her ex-husband lives in another town.
items.note: A man to whom someone was previously married.

items.example: His ex-wife works at the same company.
items.note: A woman to whom someone was previously married; an extension of the ex- pattern.

items.example: I spend time with my friends at weekends.
items.note: The natural verb–noun pattern is spend time with someone.

items.example: My neighbours get on really well.
items.note: A stronger form of get on well; often followed by with someone.

items.example: They've been a couple since they met at college.
items.note: A couple can mean two people in a romantic relationship.

items.example: My cousins are getting married next spring.
items.note: Use get married for the event; married describes the resulting state.

items.pt: namorar alguém; sair romanticamente com alguém
items.example: She went out with Daniel for a year.
items.note: Here go out with means have a romantic relationship, not simply leave the house.

items.pt: dar-se bem com um ex-parceiro; uma ex-parceira
items.example: He gets on with his ex and they still talk.
items.note: Get on with someone means have a good relationship with them.

items.example: Do you have any siblings?
items.note: A gender-neutral word for a brother or sister; a useful extension to only child.

items.example: My stepmother has two sons.
items.note: The wife of a parent who is not your biological mother; parallel to stepfather.

units.title: Unit 14 — Growing up
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate, Fourth Edition
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
units.category: People · Life stages and growing up
learningObjectives: Describe ages and life stages from birth and childhood to retirement and old age.
Give approximate ages using early, mid-, late, nearly, almost, approximately, and roughly.
Form correct age expressions including thirty years old and a thirty-year-old person.
Distinguish die/dead/alive, grow up/be brought up, and manage to.
Use allow someone to do, be allowed to do, and let someone do with correct grammar.
Describe family rules, strict parenting, leaving home, and staying out late.

items.example: The birth of their first baby was a happy occasion.
items.note: The moment when a baby is born.

items.example: Their baby is six months old.
items.note: A very young child, especially during the first year.

items.pt: criança pequena que está aprendendo a andar
items.example: The toddler is learning to climb the stairs.
items.note: A child who has recently learned to walk, often aged one to three.

items.example: Every child learns at a different speed.
items.note: The singular is child; the irregular plural is children.

items.example: I spent my childhood near the sea.
items.note: The period of life when you are a child.

items.example: The teenager enjoys playing basketball.
items.note: A person in their teens, roughly aged thirteen to nineteen.

items.pt: na adolescência; entre treze e dezenove anos
items.example: I learned to play the guitar when I was in my teens.
items.note: The period from age thirteen to nineteen.

items.example: At eighteen, she became an adult.
items.note: An adult is someone who is no longer a child; legal thresholds vary by country.

items.example: A middle-aged couple live next door.
items.note: Describes someone in the middle part of adult life; the age boundaries are approximate.

items.example: He is looking forward to retirement.
items.note: The period or act of stopping work permanently, often at an older age.

items.example: My grandmother is retired now.
items.note: Not working any more because you have retired.

items.example: He remains active in old age.
items.note: The later stage of life.

items.example: An elderly neighbour needs help with shopping.
items.note: A polite adjective for older people; avoid using it as a noun for one person.

items.example: Learning to walk is an important stage in a child's life.
items.note: A particular period in a process or in life.

items.pt: no começo dos vinte anos; com cerca de 21 a 23 anos
items.example: She started university in her early twenties.
items.note: Early twenties usually means approximately ages twenty-one to twenty-three.

items.pt: na metade dos cinquenta anos; com cerca de 54 a 56 anos
items.example: My manager is in his mid-fifties.
items.note: Mid-fifties means roughly ages fifty-four to fifty-six.

items.pt: no fim dos setenta anos; com cerca de 77 a 79 anos
items.example: My aunt is in her late seventies.
items.note: Late seventies means roughly ages seventy-seven to seventy-nine.

items.pt: na metade dos trinta anos; com cerca de 34 a 36 anos
items.example: He bought his first house in his mid-thirties.
items.note: Mid- indicates roughly the middle years of a decade.

items.example: She's nearly eighty years old.
items.note: In this context, nearly means almost, but not quite.

items.example: The children are almost ready for school.
items.note: Means very close to a state, number, or point in time.

items.example: The journey takes approximately two hours.
items.note: Means about; often used for estimates and numbers.

items.example: The ticket costs roughly twenty pounds.
items.note: An informal way to give an approximate number.

items.example: She's thirty years old.
items.note: Say She is thirty or She is thirty years old, not she has thirty.

items.example: A thirty-year-old man won the competition.
items.note: The compound adjective before a noun is singular: year-old, not years-old.

items.example: My grandfather has been dead for several years.
items.note: Dead is an adjective describing someone who is no longer living.

items.example: Both of her grandparents are still alive.
items.note: The opposite of dead; normally used after a verb such as be.

items.example: His grandfather died peacefully last year.
items.note: Die is a verb; dead is an adjective, and death is a noun.

items.pt: ser criado; ser educado durante a infância
items.example: She was brought up by her grandparents.
items.note: A passive construction meaning be raised and cared for as a child.

items.example: I grew up in a small village.
items.note: Grow up is normally intransitive; bring up is transitive or passive.

items.example: His parents were strict about bedtime.
items.note: A strict person expects rules to be followed.

items.example: The teacher doesn't allow phones in class.
items.note: Allow is followed by a person and a to-infinitive when stating permission to act.

items.example: They allow visitors to take photos.
items.note: Pattern: allow + person + to-infinitive.

items.example: Students are allowed to use a dictionary.
items.note: Passive construction: be allowed to + base verb.

items.example: We're not allowed to park here.
items.note: Use a person or group as the subject: We're not allowed to ..., rather than It's not allowed to ....

items.example: My parents let me choose my own clothes.
items.note: Let is slightly more informal than allow and is followed by an object and base verb.

items.example: Her dad lets her borrow his bicycle.
items.note: Pattern: let + person + base verb, without to.

items.pt: ficar fora de casa até tarde; voltar tarde para casa
items.example: My parents didn't let me stay out late.
items.note: Means remain away from home until a late hour.

items.pt: sair de casa; deixar a casa dos pais
items.example: She left home at eighteen to study abroad.
items.note: Here leave home means stop living in the family home.

items.example: In the end, we found a better solution.
items.note: Means finally, after a period of time or thought.

items.example: At first, the new course seemed difficult.
items.note: Refers to the beginning of a situation, often contrasted with later developments.

items.pt: conseguir fazer algo apesar da dificuldade
items.example: I managed to finish the report before lunch.
items.note: Manage to + base verb expresses success despite difficulty.

items.example: My mum was born in Wales.
items.note: Use be born, not just born, to state the event of birth.

items.example: Our coach is strict with new players.
items.note: Strict commonly combines with with for people and about for rules.

items.example: She plans to retire next summer.
items.note: Retire is the verb; retirement is the noun and retired is an adjective.

items.example: He moved abroad in his thirties.
items.note: Refers to ages thirty to thirty-nine.

items.example: People become legal adults at different ages around the world.
items.note: Become describes a change of status; legal ages differ by country.

items.example: My parents let me stay up to watch the film.
items.note: Different from stay out late, which means remain away from home.
